<!-- Why the compile path has its own standard library instead of the interpreter's, what the 2008-2012 team said about it, and what one library would cost by each of the three routes. Written 2026-09-20 by a delegated worker on Pavol's question. Evidence only: it costs the routes and recommends none. Every claim cites a file:line, a commit, or a run whose output is named. The one measurement taken live is a re-run of the prelude probe's driver under a private cache; nothing in the tree was modified except this file. -->

# Two libraries

Terms used below. **Prelude**: the set of apis the compiler implicitly imports into every component, so a program can name `ZZ32` without importing anything. **World**: a prelude plus the switches that go with it; `fortress <file>.fss` runs the interpreter's world, `fortress compile` the compiler's. **Rung**: one declaration added to a prelude with a failing test, gated on `ant testFast` and `ant testSystem`.

## 1. When the split was made, and in whose words

The compiler's prelude was born on **2008-12-19** in commit `c8d301411` by **Jan-Willem Maessen** (`jmaessen`), whose whole message is: *"[libraries, interpreter] Preliminary version of stripped-down minimalist fortress library for first crack at compilation, plus interpreter support to let it all run through gracefully."* It created `Library/CompilerLibrary.fss` (27 lines: two `print` bindings and an empty `trait String`), `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fss` (49 lines), and the world switch itself, then in `interpreter/glue/WellKnownNames.java`.

The switch was documented as provisional in the same commit, in a comment that is still in the tree at `compiler/WellKnownNames.java:109-111`: *"Re-points fortressLibrary etc. to special compiler (rather than interpreter) versions of the code. **Hopefully temporary hack as we work on importing java objects cleanly.**"* Note the stated reason: importing Java objects. Not the type checker — the first `CompilerBuiltin` still bound its natives with `builtinPrimitive` and the interpreter's glue package; `import java` arrived three months later (`b2880c05c` 2009-03-03, *"We now import java.lang.Math, but we don't use it yet"*; `2f8744701` 2009-03-09).

Three further facts from the history. A **third** prelude existed for a month — `352c78880` (EricAllen, 2009-02-06) *"Added TypeCheckerLibrary and TypeCheckerBuiltin; threaded through front-end"*, removed by `904bd2684` (sukyoungryu, 2009-03-09) *"[type checker] Eliminated type checker libraries"*; its residue is `Types.useTypeCheckerLibraries()` (`compiler/Types.java:90-92`), which now just calls `useCompilerLibraries()`. The split's maintenance cost shows up early: `ce1366c17` (2010-02-25) *"Fixed a bug in Shell: use the interpreter library instead of the compiler library when running tests with the interpreter. (Found by Chulwoo Lee)"*. And the team had a word for what it was putting in the compiler's library: *"Tested by adding **bogus** Array traits in the CompilerLibrary. Tests should be added when generic traits can be compiled"* (`ccccbe26f`, 2009-10-04), *"It should use a parameterized Generator type but it is not yet supported. Instead, we use GeneratorZZ32 for now. Added **bogus** IN and = operators"* (`525264af1`, 2009-10-02), and, a month before the wind-down, David Chase's *"Added missing CMP method to **bogo-trait** ZZ32"* (`b16964470`, 2012-06-27). `compiler/Types.java:73-76` names the pair the way they thought of it: *"the compiler libraries"* against *"the full libraries"*.

**The specification knows one library, not two.** `Specification/library/structure.tex:13-22`: the automatically imported libraries are *"chiefly `FortressLibrary` and `FortressBuiltin`"*; `library/default-libraries.tex:15-24`: *"Two sets of libraries are imported into every Fortress program by default"* — `FortressLibrary` and the builtins. `CompilerLibrary` appears in no `.tex` in the tree, and Sun's own `README.txt:432-437` says the same. The split is an implementation fact the published design never acknowledged.

**What no source says.** No commit message, no README, no text under `Papers/`, no spec `\note{}` states an intention to compile the full library one day, or any plan for ending the split. The record runs the other way: the compiler prelude was still being grown declaration by declaration in the project's last month. The wind-down note names the wall the project stopped at, and it is the same one — *"the mismatch between the (rather ambitious) Fortress type system and a virtual machine not designed to support it"* — while listing *"symmetric multiple inheritance with type exclusion"* among the eight things they were pleased with (`research/extracts/fortress-websites-wayback.md:110-123`). Exclusion is what two thirds of §3's errors are about.

## 2. What the two libraries share, and where they differ

**Sizes.** Compiler world: `CompilerLibrary.fss/.fsi` 718 + 358 lines, `CompilerBuiltin.fss/.fsi` 1,636 + 786 — 3,498 in all. Interpreter world: `FortressLibrary` 4,507 + 2,550, `FortressBuiltin` 701 + 218 — 7,976. `AnyType.fss` (17 lines) is shared. Since ladder rung 1 (`1bd8d3ad1`) the compiler prelude is four apis, not three: `compilerAlgebra()` is no longer commented out at `WellKnownNames.java:124`, which supersedes `map/dormant-code.md` §1.4. `Library/GeneratorLibrary` (469 + 314) remains unwired.

**Written twice.** Counting top-level declarations in the four api files by kind and name: 183 in the compiler world, 276 in the interpreter's, **75 in both** — 21 traits (`ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `NN64`, `RR64`, `ZZ`, `Number`, `String`, `Generator`, `Maybe`, `Range`, `Matrix`, `Comparison`, `TotalComparison`, `Reduction`, `Condition`, the exception roots), 27 objects, 9 operator names and 18 functions. The operator figure is by name and so under-reports: `opr` declaration lines alone number 346 in the compiler world's apis against 496 in the interpreter's. 108 declarations exist only in the compiler world, 63 of them the `characterXxx` category constants and the fixed-size integer bounds. **201 exist only in the interpreter's**: the array and range vocabulary (`Array`, `Array1..3`, `ImmutableArray`, `Vector`, `Indexed`, `Rank`, the `Range` family), the reductions and generators (`SumReduction`, `BigReduction`, `MonoidReduction`, `Comprehension`, `BigOperator`), the algebra above `Number` (`QQ`, `Integral`, `AnyIntegral`, `StandardTotalOrder`, `AdditiveGroup`, `MultiplicativeRing`, `LexicographicOrder`), `Thread`, and the factory and reflection functions (`array`, `matrix`, `vector`, `immutableArray`, `region`).

**The two native binding mechanisms.** The interpreter writes `builtinPrimitive("com.sun.fortress.interpreter.glue.prim.Int$Less")` as the body; the evaluator pattern-matches that literal call and substitutes the named Java class for the body (`glue/NativeApp.java:157-215`, reached only from `interpreter/evaluator/values/FunctionClosure.java:47-57`), and the class takes the evaluator's boxed `FValue`/`FObject` and returns `FBool.make(…)`. 339 such bindings in the two interpreter prelude files (108 in `FortressLibrary.fss`, 231 in `FortressBuiltin.fss`), 427 across the whole interpreter library. The compiler writes `import java com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.{simpleIntArith.intLT => jIntLT}` and then an ordinary call `jIntLT(self, other)`: 330 such aliases in 20 `import java` blocks, over 370 public static methods in 25 classes under `nativeHelpers/`.

**Could one text carry both?** Not in the `builtinPrimitive` direction: the name is declared only at `FortressBuiltin.fsi:30`, nothing under `compiler/` or `codegen/` refers to it, and a component that gives it a body compiles and then calls that body, the class-name string being inert data (`perf-probes/prelude/REPORT.md` §3, `07-builtinprimitive-probe.out`). The other direction is **not obviously blocked, and this is new here**: `ForeignJava`, which reads a Java class with ASM and synthesizes an api for it, lives in the shared `repository/` package and is wired into the *interpreter* as well as the compiler — `interpreter/Driver.java:441`, `interpreter/env/ForeignComponentWrapper.java:59`, `interpreter/env/ClosureMaker.java:64`. None of the 381 `.fss` files in `ProjectFortress/tests/`, the interpreter's own corpus, contains an `import java` line. So the mechanism is wired on both sides and exercised on one; whether an `import java` binding runs under the interpreter is one small probe that nobody has run.

**A difference that is not in the library files.** `Shell.useCompilerLibraries()` (`Shell.java:371-386`) flips three desugaring settings besides the prelude names, and one of them changes the language the text is written in: `setExtendsObjectPreDesugaring(true)` makes `PreDisambiguationDesugaringVisitor.forStaticParam` (`:134-148`) rewrite an unbounded static parameter's extends clause in the compiler world and leave it alone in the interpreter's. `Types.useCompilerLibraries()` (`compiler/Types.java:72-83`) additionally re-points `String`, `JavaString`, `Exception` and `CheckedException` from the library api to the builtin one. A shared text has to be correct under both settings, or the settings have to be reconciled first.

### 3.1 Bends and reversals

**1. Row 816, how the export check reads an api member written `abstract` (F-282; climb batch 21b's fork 20; climb batch 22's question 1, taken at its default). Bends. Reverse. Consequential.**

- The designers' sources split three ways, and I read them in P-26's order. (a) The team's text: `apis.tex:252-256`, "a definition d' ... that includes definitions for all declarations other than the methods or fields declared abstract in d", reads as needing no body, and is silent on needing a declaration; `source-code.tex:384-385`, "a satisfying trait declaration is allowed to provide a concrete declaration", reads as the member being declared either way. (b) The team's library: `String`'s api wrote `abstract splitWithOffsets()` and `abstract split()` (`a874948ac:Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:2308-2309`) with no member in the component's `trait String` and bodies in the string objects (`a874948ac:Library/FlatString.fss:146-147`, `String.fss:156-157`, `:317`); the library was never compiled by the team. (c) The team's compiled checker: `equalListMembers` refused a component whose trait had fewer members than its api (`inAPI.length > inComp.length`) and `equalFnHeaders` carried `ignoreAbstract`, which matches an abstract api header to a concrete component header; both are Chase's lines of 2012 at `5a68404fd`. The revival's `031c38bbc` wrote the count `inAPI.count(l => ! isAbstractMember(l)) > inComp.length` and the comment "So a member declared abstract in the API needs no corresponding member" (blame at `ExportChecker.scala:783-791`).
- So the implementers' later word is reading (2), and it was written against the code generator that makes a client's call an `invokeinterface` on the component's trait interface (`CodeGen.java:5089`, `:6799-6841`). This is P-26's case exactly: the text was a wish, the checker met the JVM. The library's two `String` members are the earlier practice, written for walk, which finds a method on the object by name and never needed the declaration. The worker skill already states reading (2) (`library.md:44`, `compiler.md:74`).
- The designers' own way: the component's trait declares each member its api writes `abstract`, abstract or concrete; the checker refuses one that does not.
- Cost: 1 rung, before the names batch: the checker's count restored (the planner's `export-check-alt4i.patch` is that turn), and 12 bodyless lines in the component's traits (`String`'s 7, `Range`'s `isEmpty`, `ReadableArray`'s `opr[_:TrivialOpenRange]`, `ActualReduction`'s `empty` and `join`, `AnyMaybe`'s `holds`), which walk reads as abstract and whose objects already define. Cheaper before than after: today the only cost is a distance of 1 for one rung; after the names batch every compiled client of `String`'s split, `Range`'s `isEmpty` and the others dies at the call, and compiled tests pin whatever ran. The code generator's third way (about 30 lines) is not the fix: it leaves the absent member, the other header, the narrowed return and the functional method dying, and it cannot make the checker refuse an absent member at all.
- A sibling to file, not to decide: `ReadableArray`'s subscript is defined at narrower return types by its objects, and the probe found no bridge method emitted for that shape. Whether the code generator emits a bridge for an ordinary covariant override in a trait the component declares is to be measured in the same rung.
- Record: row 816's class becomes `implementation gap (checker)` from `design limit (specification)`; F-282 is rewritten; the audit's action 6 ("leave as asked, default as landed") is overruled by this ruling.
- **Default: option 2 of the coordinator's draft ask, the component declares them.**

**2. P-75, `NN32` into `RR64`. Reverse: withdraw.** J1023 V7's reasoning is unchanged and nothing since moves it: every way to build it breaks P-74's promotion for a `ZZ32` with an `NN32` and turns two team tests red (row 575); the prelude declared no integer-to-float coercion; the WD's general sentence is early text. - F-53 **At the last landed gate, climb batch 22's, the distance to the switch-over is 0 errors and the checker count is 0.** The distance counts the compiled checker's distinct errors over the interpreter's library, its twelve apis and their twelve components, running every stage of each whatever the earlier stages reported, and classes them by root cause (F-54). POSITIONS.md:88
- P-153 **The integer power splits on the base: an integer base gives an integer or raises an error, and a float or rational base gives the fraction.** Each integer type's `^` returns its own type at every exponent. At a negative exponent, the bases 1 and -1 give their exact power, a base of 0 raises `DivisionByZero`, and any other base raises `IntegerOverflow`. A program that wants a fraction writes a float or rational base, as in `2.0^(-1)`. Why: the team's later code gives an integer power the type of its integer base at a signed exponent (P-26, the team's later work outweighs the specification's early text). Overloads choose by type, and no type tells a negative exponent from a non-negative one, since a signed integer or a numeral can be either. So the split is on the base, and the sign of the exponent is tested at run time, as the library tests a value's sign everywhere (P-80, run-time sign tests in place of sign-refined types). Row 441: the same rule on the compiled path, whose own powers give 0 at a negative exponent and a raw Java exception at a base of 0, and overflow silently or with a raw Java exception (row 523).

Its string is to name a static Java method in `nativeHelpers/`, the compiled path's helpers, such as `"com.sun.fortress.nativeHelpers.simpleIntArith.intLT"`, in place of a glue class of walk, which the compiled path cannot use (F-32). Walk is to load the named helper through a loader beside its glue classes. At the parse, before the checker, the compiled path is to rewrite each such body into a synthetic `import java` of the helper and a call, and to refuse a string that names no helper. The bindings move onto helpers step by step, and from the step that moves a binding, the compiled checker checks it against the helper's Java signature, not all at once at the switch-over. The other form, `import java` declarations written in the library itself, is not taken. Every binding still names a glue class. Row 796: walk loads a binding's string only as a glue class. Row 309: the compiled path has no counterpart of `builtinPrimitive`.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### Numbers

POSITIONS.md:84
- P-77 **Scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` only, as the compiler's prelude declares them (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi`).** Why: a JVM array has at most as many elements as the largest `ZZ32`. A range over another integer type is a static error. A loop whose counter needs a wider type runs over a `ZZ32` range and widens each element, as in `j: ZZ64 = i`. A range of rank 2 or 3 is a tuple of `ZZ32` scalar ranges. The public range traits, such as `Range[\I\]`, stay generic in their index type: the ranges of rank 2 and 3 extend them at pairs and triples of `ZZ32`.

== explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md, ## Landed semantics; it points to P-77

FACTS.md:164
- F-133 **The one library's scalar ranges are over `ZZ32` alone.** It builds P-77. In the interpreter's library, a range that reaches `ZZ32`'s minimum or maximum has the right size and elements, with no overflow, unless it is strided and a difference of its bounds leaves `ZZ32` (row 522, below). On the compiled path, the compiler library has no strided range (row 514), and its range `IN` and `=` are always `false` (rows 479, 481). When the compiled checker reads the one library, as every compiled program will after the switch-over, a `case` with no comparison operator compares by `=` where the specification gives ∈, so the clause never matches. This holds where the guard is typed by a type variable bounded by a `Contains` type (the library's trait of a membership `IN`, which ranges extend), or by a union of them (row 480); over the compiler library the checker picks ∈. POSITIONS.md:81
- P-74 **Mixed integer widths convert by declared coercions: each wider integer type declares a `coerce` from each narrower integer type, as the compiler prelude does.** A conversion that is exact is implicit, and a conversion that can lose precision is written out. So `ZZ32` values and integer numerals coerce into `RR64` implicitly, and a `ZZ64` value into `RR64` is written out (P-66, Java's defaults corrected where they lose precision). A call of a generic function with arguments of mixed widths infers, on both paths, the narrowest type into which its arguments coerce. A range is over `ZZ32` only (P-77, the rule on ranges). The specification's `widens` declaration, which would make a narrow computation stored into a wide variable run wide, is deferred. ## 3. Row 816 and P-158 (10-25 19:06 to 10-26 04:28)

**The argument, in the order he asked for it (19:35:13):**

1. *The two paths call a method differently.* Walk finds a method on the object by name at the call; the trait need not declare it. The compiled path calls through the trait's Java interface; if the trait does not declare the method, the call dies with `NoSuchMethodError`.
2. *The team's two libraries each followed their path.* The compiler's prelude: the api writes `abstract loop(body: ZZ32->()): ()` in `GeneratorZZ32`; the component restates `loop(body: ZZ32->()): ()` with no body; the objects give the body (`Library/CompilerLibrary.fsi:112-120`, `.fss:301-312`). Chase's 2012 export check (`5a68404fd`) enforced it: a component trait with fewer members than its api trait is refused. The interpreter's library, written for walk and never compiled by the team, sometimes leaves an api's `abstract` member out of the component's trait (`String`'s `split`), and walk does not care.
3. *What the revival changed.* When the checker read the interpreter's library, Chase's check refused 12 such members. Two ways: (a) add the 12 declarations to the components, the compiled library's way; (b) weaken the check. Climb batch 21b's rung E took (b) (`031c38bbc`), from a misreading of `apis.tex` ("includes definitions for all declarations other than … abstract" read as "needs no member", where it says "needs no body"). The chain: an Opus ways worker of 10-20 (`reviews/array-sites-ways.md`, "4i", "Decision: none, since it is the text's own rule"); the export probe of 10-23 built it; batch 21's planner made it fork 20 with the default "the team's own text"; its Fable review and I passed it as not consequential; rung E built it; its skeptic found the `NoSuchMethodError` after the build; the 21b review kept it as "it cannot happen yet"; batch 22 carried it as question 1 and I launched batch 22 at about 02:01 on 10-24 without sending him the question. No document before the change mentions `NoSuchMethodError`. Root cause: one sentence misread; nobody read the code it changed (Chase's deliberate count) or asked what a compiled call does; the change cleared errors, which was the batch's goal.
4. *The fix (his option 2).* Restore Chase's count; add 12 bodyless declarations to five component traits (`String` 7: `depth`, `isBalanced`, `verify`, `rangeContains`, `balanced`, `splitWithOffsets`, `split`; `Range`'s `isEmpty`; `ReadableArray`'s `opr[_:TrivialOpenRange]`; `ActualReduction`'s `empty` and `join`; `AnyMaybe`'s `holds`). No body, not an empty body: an empty body makes the method concrete, and then no object must define it.

**His decision:** option 2 (19:06:08 on 10-25); his reason (04:28:41 on 10-26): "by the standing position that later team's work supersedes earlier one, we take the compiled path's way over the walk library's. That's why 21b should have chosen (a), not weaken the check — we must reverse this." Recorded as P-158 (`edbd0d4f5`, reason `5da8144e4`); F-282 and row 816 rewritten; PLAN's phase 4 line "Row 816's repair". At 07:30:36 he placed the repair in climb batch 22c (section 6).

- P-44 **`AnyIntegral` stays closed by its `comprises` clause, and the compiled checker reads the clause as the team's 2012 texts do.** The library's `AnyIntegral`, whose `comprises` clause lists the five integer types `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64`, stays closed. Beside the clause stays a comment in the team's `NOT YET` form, by which the team's library records a clause that it cannot write yet: here `comprises Integral[\I\] where [\I\]`, whose `where` form is not built. `Integral[\I\]` extends `AnyIntegral` and is not in the list. The checker accepts such a generic trait below a closed trait when every type that the checker knows below it is listed. The clause's text in the library, and walk, stay as they are. Why: the team's 2012 texts, Luchangco's Types chapter and Welterweight, are its later word (P-25, P-26), and by them the clause is right as written. The rule leaves a hole that every way of closing `AnyIntegral` shares, except the team's 2008 way, a `comprises` clause on `Integral[\I\]` itself: a program's own subtype of `Integral`, declared in another component, is accepted although no listed type is above it. Row 487 records the hole, and this decision does not close it.
- P-47 **Each integer type declares its own `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX`, instead of relying on those that it inherits from the generic order traits.** The integer types are the five that `AnyIntegral` lists: `ZZ32`, `ZZ64`, `ZZ`, `NN32` and `NN64`. Through `Integral`, each inherits the three operators from `StandardTotalOrder` and the `StandardMin`, `StandardMax` and `StandardMinMax` that it extends. `a MINMAX b` is the pair `(a MIN b, a MAX b)`. The `MAX` that a `ZZ64` inherits types `self` as the order trait, so neither it nor `QQ`'s `MAX` is more specific. Under walk, `b MAX 1` for a `ZZ64` `b` would then stop the run with "Ambiguous coercion". With their own declarations, these operators answer at the type that their arguments promote to (P-74), as `b + 1` does. Why: it is the library's own device. `QQ`, `RR64` and the compiler's prelude declare all three, and the specification's `ZZ` declares its own `MIN` and `MAX`.
- P-76 **An integer numeral has a type of its own, `IntLiteral`, which each number type converts from: in the interpreter's library now, and under walk once walk has the checker's static types.** The design is the compiler's prelude's working one, taken in place of the specification's numeral types, which the team left unfinished. Why the split: walk has no static types, so it would give a list of numerals the element type `IntLiteral`, with no declared type to go by. The interpreter's library declares `IntLiteral`, the conversions from it into the five integer types, `QQ` and `RR64`, and `IntLiteral`'s own arithmetic, which the team had left commented out until coercion existed. Walk still gives an integer numeral the type `ZZ32`, or `ZZ64` or `ZZ` when its value does not fit, so no numeral reaches `IntLiteral`'s declarations under walk. Walk gaps: a numeral that walk matches as a `ZZ32` in a `typecase` or an overload (row 79), a numeral at an `NN32` or `NN64` binding (row 454), an integer numeral beyond `ZZ32`'s range at an `RR64` binding (row 443), a `nat` parameter used as a value (row 486), and coercion through tuple and varargs parameters (rows 395 and 511).
- P-152 **Walk and the compiled checker read the exclusion of two generic declarations over their whole parameter types, by existential reduction.** With static parameters, the parameter types of two declarations can exclude each other as a whole, even where no single parameter excludes its counterpart. In `o[\T\](x: P[\T\], b: Box[\T\])` beside `o[\T\](x: Q[\T\], b: Box[\T\])`, where `P[\T\]` excludes `Q[\T\]` only at the same `T`, neither parameter excludes alone. But no value is a `Box` of two types, so `b` fixes the same `T` for both declarations, and no argument fits both. A generic trait in `Box`'s place fixes `T` in the same way. Both paths read such a pair as excluding, and judge it on that reading by the overloading rules (P-45: the 2011 paper's No Duplicates, Meet and Return Type rules). Why: the type group's 2011 paper decides exclusion between parameter types with static parameters by existential reduction (`Papers/Types/exc-reduction.tick`; P-26, the type group's later word outweighs the specification's early text), as the revised specification states (`Specification/advanced/overloading.tex`, "Declarations with Static Parameters"). Walk refuses such a pair at load where one declaration has a `where` clause, which the checker accepts (row 787); and walk reads an object type over a static parameter, such as `Box[\T\]`, as excluding a type that it equals at some instance, such as `Box[\ZZ32\]`, so that it loads a pair that the checker refuses (row 788).
- P-48 **A type parameter that a call's arguments do not fix takes its bound, never `Bottom`.** The arguments leave a parameter unfixed when it occurs only in the result type; when two arguments meet at it with no narrowest type into which both convert (a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` have one, `ZZ64`, by P-74); or when dispatch, at run time, picks a generic declaration and must choose the instance to run. Its instance is then the intersection of its upper bounds (`Any` if it has none). At checking, that is narrowed by what the call's expected type (P-49 defines it) requires of the declared return type; at run time, by the static type that the checker gave the call. It is never `Bottom`, never the union of the arguments' types, and never the value's type alone. The rule sets the instance, not which declaration runs (P-46). Why: the rule is the team's later word, from the POPL 2019 paper on multiple dispatch, and the curator trusts the team's later work above his own understanding (P-26). The rule changes nothing in microGPT, whose types are concrete. The library keeps the team's declarations of `fail`, `builtinPrimitive` and `List`'s empty comprehension, whose type parameters have no written bound, without the `extends Object` that a batch had added. Under walk, which has no static types, dispatch takes the value's type. Row 538: a compiled dispatcher that carries the static type that the checker gave the call, so that a generic declaration reached only at run time gets this instance. Rows 587, 591 and 612: three cases in which walk still gives `Bottom`.

- P-17 **Unboxed doubles and arrays of unboxed doubles are required: without them the revival misses its point.** Why: a language meant for high performance cannot box its numbers. Today the code generator boxes every number: an `RR64` value is an object of the class `FRR64`. In Java models of microGPT's three array kernels, the dot product, the matrix product and the row lift, boxing is the main cost (F-11 holds the measurement). How arrays store doubles, as `double[]`, is P-84's decision.
- P-84 **An `RR64` array is stored as a Java `double[]`, unboxed, and arrays keep the team's `nat` sizes in their types.** Why: a high-performance language cannot box its array elements, and the sizes are central to the team's design. So the storage and the sizes are one design: the sizes stay in the array types as `nat` static parameters, as the library's `Vector` and `Matrix` declare them, and the compiled checker checks them. The sizes do not wait while a first version of the store carries them only as run-time fields; that layered plan was rejected. Both halves follow the library's own patterns (P-27, the library's own practice is the standard). The compiled checker checks `nat` static parameters (F-67). The compiled path's `double[]` store waits with the other array decisions until after the switch-over; among them is decision A, how an `RR64` array made through the library's generic array traits gets that store (P-85).
- P-85 **The array design's three questions are open, with no default, and return after the switch-over with the array decisions A, B and D.** The array design is the compiled path's design for arrays. The three questions: whether the array factory chooses a store for each element type; whether the store also keeps the size as a field, beside the size in the type; and whether a factory for a size known only at run time returns the unsized `Array[\E,I\]`, whose type holds no size. These questions are apart from decisions A, B and D: decision A is how an `RR64` array made through the library's generic array traits gets the `double[]` store (P-84), B is where unboxed arithmetic happens, and D is the sizes in the model's own types (P-87). The whole preparation for the array work is to be done before the switch-over; only the work itself waits.

## 6. Side findings

- **The audit's exclusion list is short by two commits.** `zero-audit.md`, B.1, "Excluded", lists the prelude commits `cee79d3f1` to `4ed46558d`, `6bec1b004` and `ce0c7f453`. - **A cast's exception kind differs between the two libraries.** The prelude has `object CastException extends UncheckedException` (`CL.fsi:83`). $\begin{array}{l}
{\bf trait}~{\tt Ring}\ob{X <: {\tt Number}}~{\bf comprises}~X~\dots~{\bf end}\\
{\bf trait}~{\tt Field}\ob{X <: {\tt Number}}~{\bf comprises}~X~{\bf extends}~{\tt Ring}\ob{X}~\dots~{\bf end}
\end{array}$\\

The self-type idiom is realized with the {\bf comprises} clause which contains the instantiation of the self type.
The {\bf comprises} clause limits the types that can extend the given type to those appearing in the clause.
In this idiomatic usage, the type ${\tt Ring}\ob{X}$ is identified as $X$.  Thus a ${\tt Field}\ob{\mathbb{Q}}$
is really just $\mathbb{Q}$ itself.

The question for him: which way makes the 30 check without changing what walk computes.

## 2. What the sources say, in the order his decisions weigh them

1. **The library.** The 29 bodies of shapes A and B are the team's, present at the import of 2012-07-19 (`5a68404fd`), but for the six that the revival wrote in the same shape (`:688-690`, `d846e3644`; `:2183`, `:2187`, `f3b62bc83`; ways note section 1). The team wrote them as the orders' and the algebra's **minimal complete definitions**, the documented set of methods a type must define to get the rest for free: "Minimal complete definition: CMP or { <, = }" (`:217-218`), "either CMP or <" (`:274`), "Must define + and either unary or binary -" (`:355`). Two team tests rely on them (`ProjectFortress/tests/parametricManiaCompr.fss:20-23`, `parametricListCompr.fss:18`). The interpreter's library has no self type anywhere.
2. **The team's compiled world.** The compiler's library spells its orders with the idiom, `trait StandardTotalOrder[\T\] ... comprises T` and `trait Equality[\T\] comprises T` (`Library/CompilerAlgebra.fsi:16`, `:24`), with abstract operators only. Three gated team tests exercise the checker's self type today: `Compiled10.l` and `Compiled10.m` type-check (`AfterTypeChecking.test:33`), and `XXX10k.test` pins the checker's reading of `Compiled10.k` message by message, `self` typed `(T[\U\] & {U})`, `j(self)` with `j(x:U)` accepted and `k(self)` refused (`XXX10k.test:13-29`; `Compiled10.k.fss:14-21`, the team's own statement of the rule). And one breadcrumb: `Compiled17ee.fss` (copyright 2010) is the team's copy of the library's orders into a compiled test, the parameter renamed `Self`, with the same `MIN`, `MAX` and `MINMAX` bodies as `:287-290` and no `comprises Self` (`:167-180`); no `.test` file drives it (`Compiled17defgh.test:10` drives `17d`, `17e`, `17h`, `17i`). Why it was shelved is not recorded. Nels Beckman's 2008 test diagnoses the same shape: "the type of other needs to be APO[\Self\] rather than Self" (`not_working_static_tests/SelfTypeTest.fss:15-18`).
3. **The type group's late positions** (POSITIONS, "The type group's late positions outweigh the early text"). They do not speak with one voice here.
   - Welterweight (2012) types `self` in a trait as the plain trait type `T[P]` (`Papers/Welterweight/fig-wellformeddecls.tick:55`), admits only constructed types in a `comprises` clause (`fig-grammar.tick:6-8`, `:33-37`), and leaves its "Self-typed generics" dispatch step commented out with the placeholder "{\it Explanation of how this works}" (`dispatch.tick:195-210`).
   - Naden (2012-08-31, the latest dated text): "The self-type idiom is realized with the comprises clause ... the type Ring[X] is identified as X" (`justificationOfRTR.tex:580-582`); and, after showing that the idiom as a first-class type breaks the Return Type Rule on the nested tower, "the self-type idiom should be more than simply an idiom and instead a separate construct which cannot be used as a first class type, but instead only in bounds" (`:626-630`).
   - POPL 2019 has no self types and no tower (`research/extracts/ParkPOPL2019-extract.md:280`, `:328-329`).
   - The later Types chapter says nothing of `self`; its `comprises` sentence lists "types and generic types determined by the generic type of the declaration" (`types.tick:384-389`), and Luchangco's comment beside it wants every listed type to be a trait type (`:245`).
- Library only, 21 lines, clears 29; the team's own `cast[\T\]` (`:33-37`) and the team's own typecase on a trait's parameter inside its functional method (`Contains.MATCH`, `:1093-1098`). Nothing else changes.
- Against it. It is Java's answer: a static fact becomes a run-time check, at every call of every default body, and it tells the checker nothing, so every future body of the same shape pays it again. It is a per-site patch repeated 21 times, which is the "rule slapped on a rule" his position refuses, and it reads as the user-side workaround his library rule rules out. Its deciding unknown is walk's binding of a trait's parameter inside a functional method's body (ways note, way 2), and whether the code generator compiles a cast at a trait's parameter in a default body is unmeasured (row 426 covers a function's parameter only).
- Its place: the fallback if the recommended way's one measurement fails (section 6).

### Way 5: the team's idiom, `comprises T` on seven traits

- What it has. It is the team's own built device (Ryu, 2009, `3a8ad3b67`; Allen, 2011, `dbc91f830`), its meaning is already in the specification (`var-ref.tex:63-69`), the compiler library spells it, and Naden's 2012 text names it as the realisation of the idiom. The checker needs no change.
- What it costs. Three areas move. The library: one clause on each of seven traits in two files (the hierarchy rule forces `LexicographicOrder`, `MultiplicativeRing` and the orders to carry it together, `traits.tex:241-248`; route C's experiment found the same, "the clauses go on the whole family or on none of it", `route-c-experiment.md:104`). Walk: it overflows its stack at load on any `comprises T` (row 407, `FType.java:280-294`), so a 6-line edit in `BuildEnvironments.finishTrait` must land first, with its test; under that edit `Integral[\ZZ32\]` records `comprises { ZZ32 }`, so walk's exclusion verdicts at load can move (`anyintegral-comprises-ways.md`, way 3). The specification: it must legalise a type variable in a `comprises` clause, which the Working Draft's text does not admit ("a declared trait identifier") and the type group's 2012 calculus dropped from its grammar; the revival's `comprises` rung left exactly that door shut on purpose (`decision-record.md:48`, rejected wording 4).
- Its risk. The clause does more than type `self`: it closes each trait to its parameter, which changes exclusion and the hierarchy checks for every instantiation. On the nested tower, eight such clauses overflowed the checker's api overloading check in `Formula.tImplies`/`primImp` under an exclusion question, with the forest rule dropped as well (FACTS, "Route C built whole as a shadow"; `route-c-experiment.md:136`). The flat library is unmeasured. The one-trait form (a) finishes the count stage at 87 (`anyintegral-comprises-ways.md`, way 3) and reaches 7 sites.
- Against the record. It is the first self type in the library's text under route A, and the record's reading of route A is "no self type enters the library" (`CLIMB-BATCH-8.md:113`). Whether that reading is his is for him to say; section 7.

# Trap test: the key

For the grader. Two readers answered `questions.md` as the coordinating session, each in its own copy of the repository. One copy holds today's POSITIONS entries. The other holds the rewritten ones, with today's texts moved to `POSITIONS-history.md`. You score blind to the copy. Paths are under `explorations/` unless they start with `ProjectFortress/`, `Library/`, `Specification/`, `Specification-1.0-frozen/`, `Papers/` or `.claude/`. "Row N" is a gap-ledger row (`coordinator/tools/facts-extract.sh 'ledger:N'`). "The coordinator skill" is `.claude/skills/coordinator/SKILL.md`.

**Scoring** (the kit's rubric, `coordinator/process-engineering/record-test/key.md`). **Decision 0-2**: 2, the decision is right and rests on the facts below; 1, right in the main but missing a fact that changes a step or a ground; 0, wrong, or a step that cannot work, or a decision of the curator's contradicted, or a re-measurement of what the record holds. **Sources 0-1**: 1, every load-bearing fact beyond the quoted entries is cited to a source that holds it (the sources below, or an equivalent one), or the answer needed none; 0, such a fact is asserted without a source, invented, or the answer stops at the quoted entries where they could not carry it.

A reader who reaches the right decision by a ground in the wrong layer (below, his words of 05:25) gets at most 1 for the decision: the test is whether the record orients the coordinator's judgement, not only its verdict.

## The curator's words that the key rests on

UTC, 2026-10-25 and 2026-10-26, cleaned of dictation slips. The transcript holds them; `coordinator/POSITIONS-history.md` holds the one of 04:28 under P-158.

1. **The three layers** (10-26 05:25): what Fortress does, against how Fortress is implemented on the JVM, and, related, interoperability with Java. The rule as he approved it at 07:42: a ground from one layer does not decide a question in another. A sentence of the specification is not by itself the reason for a setting of the compiled path, and an implementation limit is not by itself a rule of the language.
2. **The compiled path's way, where the team's later work backs it** (10-26 04:28, on row 816): "by the standing position that later team's work supersedes earlier one, we take the compiled path's way over the walk library's. That's why 21b should have chosen (a), not weaken the check — we must reverse this." Option (a) was to add the declarations to the components, as the compiler's prelude does. Recorded as P-158.
3. **Porting back is allowed** (10-26 07:30): "if the divergence between the compiler and the interpreter was that we need to port something from the compiler library back to the interpreter library that is allowed. For example, we did this with the numerics, flattening of the numeric tower. … I'm not sure whether we were just always extending the compiler to accept whatever was written in the interpreter library, or whether we were porting the legitimate changes from the compiler library back to the interpreter library." The caution that he accepted (his "Yes. Exactly." at 07:36): not everything in the compiler's prelude is a design. The team built it as a "stripped-down minimalist fortress library for first crack at compilation" (`c8d301411`), and called parts of it "bogus" and a "bogo-trait" (`coordinator/two-libraries.md`, section 1). Each prelude choice is sorted into a deliberate design, with its commit, author and date, or a stub for the bootstrap; a stub is not the team's later word.
4. **The goal of the switch-over** (10-26 04:47): "The whole point of the switch-over is to avoid the need to port walk's library into the compiler's library. The revival is continuing the development of the type checker, so that it would accept the fuller Fortress library that the interpreter uses."
5. **The flat number types rest on the exclusion rule** (10-26 07:46), not on the compiler prelude's history.
